analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally buy cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and Europe.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 8 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has had no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Department to write rules letting wholesale distributors, pharmacies, and individual patients import prescription drugs from Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and European Union countries, where the same drugs often sell for much less than in the United States. It drops the current requirement that the Secretary certify importation poses no added safety risk, expands the types of drugs that can be imported to include insulin and biologics, lets individuals fill U.S. prescriptions at certified foreign pharmacies for up to a 90-day personal supply, and bars manufacturers from discriminating against sellers who export to the U.S. It also adds criminal penalties for websites selling counterfeit drugs or dispensing without a prescription.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. prices for prescription drugs, especially the tens of millions who report skipping or not filling prescriptions because of cost. Patients could buy the same active ingredients at the lower prices charged abroad, including insulin and other biologics, with a certified-seller list, testing labs, and tracing rules meant to keep counterfeit drugs out. Community pharmacies and wholesale distributors that import could compete on price.

how_it_helps.text: Drug prices in the U.S. average 2.78 times comparable OECD countries, and 4.22 times for patented drugs; the bill would let importers buy the same drugs at those lower foreign prices.

The bill expands eligible imports to include insulin, biologics, intravenously infused drugs, and peritoneal dialysis solution — categories currently excluded — and lowers the personal-import hurdle so individuals can fill a U.S. prescription at a certified foreign pharmacy for a 90-day supply without a waiver.

The bill includes safety machinery: certified foreign sellers pay fees that fund oversight, laboratories test imported drugs for chemical authenticity, the Secretary can suspend importers with patterns of noncompliance, and selling counterfeit drugs or dispensing without a valid prescription online becomes a crime carrying up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. prices are propped up by the importation ban; the bill specifically outlaws charging higher prices to exporters, cutting off supply to sellers, or tweaking U.S. formulations to dodge importation. The FDA takes on new certification and enforcement duties, though certification fees from foreign sellers are meant to cover program costs.

drawbacks.text: Safety risk is the core objection: HHS for years declined to certify importation, citing risks of contamination and counterfeiting, and the bill removes that certification gate entirely, relying instead on seller certification, testing, and the Secretary's suspension powers.

If U.S. buyers tap foreign supplies at scale, exporting countries could face shortages or price pressure of their own, and manufacturers might restrict foreign sales in response — the bill's anti-discrimination rules attempt to prevent that but could provoke supply conflicts abroad.

The enforcement and testing apparatus — certifying sellers, approving labs, tracing imports — is a real administrative burden, and the bill funds it through fees on the foreign sellers it regulates, which could limit participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings for patients are large, given how much higher U.S. drug prices are than prices abroad, and the bill builds in testing, certification, tracing, and criminal penalties for counterfeits rather than opening the border wholesale. The honest tradeoff is that it removes the safety certification that HHS used as the gate for years, so the protection depends on how well the new certification and testing system is run. The bigger obstacle is political: with no bipartisan support in evidence, the bill is unlikely to advance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 1, 2025 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no markup, hearing, or floor vote so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill with 5 original cosponsors on May 1, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Eight Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear on the cosponsor list.
No further action appears in the bill's history since the referral — no committee markup, hearing, or vote has been recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the importation ban that sustains higher U.S. prices remains in place because the bill has not advanced, and the committee it sits in has taken up no action on it.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled five original cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Cohen, Doggett, Omar, Pingree, and Pocan
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Three additional Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Brought the cosponsor total to 8, all Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote has been scheduled in the months since introduction.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed prescription drug importation measures, arguing they undermine safety and supply chains.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 cosponsors are Democrats; there is no Republican support in the record, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill attacks the price gap that makes U.S. drug prices 2.78 times comparable countries' — it would let importers buy the same drugs abroad and bans manufacturers from raising exporter prices, restricting supplies, or altering U.S. formulations to dodge importation. This is the industry the bill is aimed at.

industries.industry: U.S. wholesale distributors and community pharmacies
industries.note: Registered importers would gain a new legal channel to buy qualifying drugs at lower foreign prices and resell to American patients, competing on price with manufacturers' U.S. list prices.

industries.industry: Licensed foreign pharmacies in Canada, the UK, EU, and Switzerland
industries.note: Certified foreign pharmacies become the sanctioned channel for U.S. personal imports of up to a 90-day supply, paying fees for certification and oversight.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Energy and Commerce Committee with no recorded action and no Republican cosponsors. Comparable importation bills have repeatedly died in committee even when drug pricing was prominent, so unless leadership elevates it or it is attached to a larger package, it is likely to stall for the rest of this Congress.
